conbody.p: History is the last section of the artifact's detail panel, below its links and figures. It is the artifact's record: what OpenV wrote down each time the artifact changed, and what people have said about it, newest first. A new version, a status move, a link added or removed, a figure replaced, a test result recorded — each leaves an entry, alongside the notes members write themselves.
Three buttons above the list decide what you are reading:

ul.li: All — the whole record, changes and comments interleaved.
Changes — only what OpenV recorded. This is the audit trail: who changed what, and when.
Comments — only what people wrote. This is the review discussion.

conbody.p: It opens on Comments, which is what most people come to it for; the recorded changes are the backdrop.

Add a comment in the box under the History heading. Use it for review discussion rather than editing the requirement text itself — the text is the requirement, the comment is what you think of it. Writing one while reading Changes switches you back to Comments, so you can see what you just added.

section.title: Deleted artifacts
section.p: Deleting an artifact keeps its history. A link to it (from Activity, a notification or a link someone shared) still opens it: read-only, marked deleted with the date it was deleted, at its last version. History lists every version, and Preview shows any of them with the links it had then. A deleted artifact cannot be edited or restored from here.

section.title: Read and unread comments
section.p: Needs you, on Home, lists the comments you have not read. Comments count as read once you see them here: as soon as the History comes into view, or straight away when you came from a Needs you line. A comment written since you last read the artifact's comments shows New.

To keep a comment in Needs you for later, click Mark unread on it. That comment, and every comment written after it on the same artifact, show Unread and stay in Needs you until you open them again or mark them read there. Your own comments are never unread to you.

section.title: Tagging inside a comment
section.p: A comment can name people and point at things, with the same two-marker convention the descriptions use.

ul.li: @ offers the people on the project. Choosing one writes the name the mention resolves to, which matters: a handle typed from memory can name nobody at all, and there is nothing to see when it does. The person is notified.

@@ names someone and raises a to-do for them as the comment is posted — the comment's first paragraph becomes the to-do, assigned to whoever it named and linked back to this artifact. Use it when you already know you are asking for something rather than talking. The to-do goes on the project's to-do list, not the board (see Kanban board, To-dos).
# and ## cite a figure or an artifact, exactly as they do in a description, and the citation is a link a reader can follow.

section.p: Raising a to-do after a comment is posted still works and has not changed: the Add to-do control on a comment that names somebody lets you set the text, the person and a due date. @@ is the shortcut, not a replacement — it takes the note's first paragraph as the to-do and no due date.
